1.rag_answer:
Viruses use the machinery and metabolism of a host cell to produce multiple copies of themselves and assemble within the cell. To do this, they enter the cell—either through receptor-mediated endocytosis or direct fusion with the cell membrane—provided the cell has the appropriate receptor on its surface. 

Most DNA viruses depend on the host cell's RNA processing machinery as well as its DNA and RNA synthesising machinery. In eukaryotes, the viral genome must cross the cell's nuclear membrane to access this machinery, while in bacteria, it only needs to enter the cell. In bacteria, bacterial polymerase translates viral mRNA into proteins, which then become helper proteins (which help assemble new virions), new virions, or proteins involved in cell lysis. Some viruses with larger genomes may encode much of this machinery themselves.
